node.label: Donna R. Gabaccia
node.date_label: We Are What We Eat (1998) · Italy’s Many Diasporas (2000) · Foreign Relations (2012) · Gender and International Migration, with Katharine M. Donato (2015)
node.description: Donna R. Gabaccia argues in Foreign Relations: American Immigration in Global Perspective (2012) that U.S. immigration must be understood through the interaction of migrants’ continuing ties abroad with American diplomacy and trade. We Are What We Eat (1998) traces immigrant and ethnic eating in the United States and Americans’ long readiness to cross boundaries of taste and identity through food. Reviewing Foreign Relations in 2015, Björn A. Schmidt welcomed its transnational perspective but criticized its imprecise concept of xenophobia and insufficient engagement with research on racism. Italy’s Many Diasporas (2000) places Italian migration in a wider transnational frame. Her joint research with Franca Iacovetta and Fraser Ottanelli connects labour migration, class, ethnicity and gender, while Gender and International Migration (2015), with Katharine M. Donato, challenges the idea that substantial female migration is a recent development.
node.representative_figures_and_works: We Are What We Eat: Ethnic Food and the Making of Americans (1998); Italy’s Many Diasporas (2000); Women, Gender, and Transnational Lives: Italian Workers of the World (2002), co-edited with Franca Iacovetta; “Laboring Across National Borders” (2004), with Franca Iacovetta and Fraser Ottanelli; Foreign Relations: American Immigration in Global Perspective (2012); Gender and International Migration: From the Slavery Era to the Global Age (2015), with Katharine M. proposed_edges.relationship: Gabaccia and Franca Iacovetta co-edited Women, Gender, and Transnational Lives (2002) and coauthored, with Fraser Ottanelli, “Laboring Across National Borders” (2004).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: UTP/JSTOR book author and joint-introduction credits, pp. 3–42; RSA Journal p. 89 explicitly identifies the edited collection. Cambridge 2004 article author list and abstract checked. Collaboration is undirected; Ottanelli’s equal article credit is retained. Complete book and article bodies unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Dirk Hoerder’s chapter in A World Connecting, 1870–1945 (2012), edited by Rosenberg, Gabaccia asks whether the volume’s essays on states, empire, trade and cultural exchange absorbed migration history; Rosenberg’s 2013 response acknowledges these possible missed opportunities.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Gabaccia pp. 20–21, especially the final two paragraphs; Rosenberg p. 29 expressly summarizes the objection as “missed opportunities” for essays to address one another. A qualified critique of editorial integration alongside praise for the collection; no claim that Rosenberg wrote the other contributors’ essays. Original chapters unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Foreign Relations (2012) connects migrants’ continuing transnational ties with U.S. diplomacy and trade, treating immigration as an enduring relationship between the United States and the wider world.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Princeton University Press description: immigrants 'were not isolationists who cut ties to their countries of origin', and the book 'takes a comprehensive look at the links between American immigration and U.S. foreign relations' as 'a brand-new global history'; the quoted Choice notice frames it as 'trade relations'. Publisher-level reading; book body unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Immigration and diplomacy in global history

proposed_edges.relationship: In Gender and International Migration (2015), Donato and Gabaccia argue that female migration has a long history and interpret changes in migrant gender composition through gender relations and political and economic conditions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Joint introduction pp. 1–2, publisher PDF: “feminization is not a recent development”; publisher date and coauthors checked. The field contribution is joint, and its claim is about the historical variability of gender composition, not proof from the unread empirical chapters.

proposed_edges.relationship: We Are What We Eat (1998) is a history of immigrant and ethnic eating in the United States, showing Americans’ long-term readiness to cross boundaries of taste and identity through food.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Harvard publisher description displayed on JSTOR, paragraphs 1–3, read in full: marketplace as an “arena for defining and expressing ethnic identities”. Description supports this bounded contribution; book unread beyond displayed chapter openings.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Laboring Across National Borders” (2004), Gabaccia, Iacovetta and Ottanelli use Italian labour migration to examine class, ethnicity and gender in the formation of modern national states.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge abstract, both paragraphs, and issue metadata: “transnational analysis of class, ethnicity, and gender”. Original print date 2004; 2005 is the online date. Joint argument and abstract-only reading retained; article body unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2013 H-Diplo review of Dirk Hoerder’s chapter in A World Connecting, 1870–1945 (2012), Gabaccia compares Hoerder’s account of nationalism with the state-formation dynamics of Maier’s “Leviathan 2.0” in the same volume and asks how Maier would assess the significance of mass labour migrations for the state-building he describes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Roundtable XIV-40 (15 July 2013), read in full on the H-Diplo/ISSF copy. Gabaccia review p. 20, paragraph beginning “But states also matter”: Hoerder’s distinction between earlier national consciousness and later chauvinism “invites comparison to the dynamics of state formation that are outlined in Charles S. Maier’s “Leviathan 2.0.”” p. 21, paragraph beginning “By calling attention to how effectively Hoerder’s account”: awareness of mobility in the essays on state, empire, trade and culture “requires greater thought”, then “How, for example, would Maier assess the significance of the mass labor migrations on the state-building dynamics that are his focus?” A qualified, named question about Maier’s chapter inside a review of Hoerder’s; she calls the volume “this very worthwhile collection”. Maier’s chapter unread; no claim that it ignores migration altogether. The p. 21 paragraph also supports gab_w_04 (to Rosenberg as editor); this edge rests on the Maier-specific sentences only.

proposed_edges.relationship: Introducing the 2013 H-Diplo roundtable on A World Connecting, 1870–1945 (2012), Iriye, co-editor of the History of the World series, quotes Gabaccia’s question whether culture travels differently when mediated rather than carried by people, calls it of key importance for the volume, and extends her call for dialogue between histories of trade and migration to histories of the state, imperialism and global cultures.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: H-Diplo Roundtable XIV-40, Introduction by Akira Iriye, pp. 3–4, paragraph beginning “Fourth, at the end of the spectrum from power-holders”: “as Donna Gabaccia points out, there are many ways of mass absorption into global culture”; quotes her question (“does culture travel differently when it is mediated …?”) and says “This is a fascinating question, which is of key importance for a volume like this”; quotes her call to “bring increasingly rich historiographies on trade and migration into a livelier and more extensive dialogue” and adds “To which we may add the historiographies on the modern state, on imperialism, and on global cultures.” Iriye introduces himself on p. 2 as co-editor, with Osterhammel, of the six-volume History of the World. An engaged response to her review, not a statement of debt either way; undirected comparison. Thin (one paragraph) but individualized: Iriye discusses each reviewer’s point separately.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Franca Iacovetta, Gabaccia edited Borders, Conflict Zones, and Memory: Scholarly Engagements with Luisa Passerini (a Women’s History Review special issue, 2016; book edition 2018), a tribute to Passerini’s scholarship that closes with a conversation co-authored by Passerini, Gabaccia and Iacovetta.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Routledge publisher page read: editors Gabaccia and Iacovetta; description opens “This volume pays tribute to Luisa Passerini, whose scholarship has had a major impact on feminist and other scholars around the world” and states the book “was originally published as a special issue of Women's History Review”; contents list the editors’ introduction, Passerini’s “Response on Borders, Conflict Zones, and Memory”, and the final chapter, “‘Bodies Across Borders. Oral And Visual Memory in Europe and Beyond’ (BABE): a conversation with Luisa Passerini, Donna Gabaccia, and Franca Iacovetta”. DOI registration metadata (Crossref) gives the journal versions: introduction, Women’s History Review 25.3 (2016), 345–364 (doi:10.1080/09612025.2015.1071567); Passerini response, 447–457; conversation, 458–469 (doi:10.1080/09612025.2015.1071564, online November 2015), authors Passerini, Gabaccia, Iacovetta. The Taylor & Francis article pages returned 403 and the EUI repository record returned 403: the introduction, response and conversation bodies are unread. The claim is limited to the editing and joint authorship; no claim that Passerini influenced Gabaccia’s own work. Dating: special issue 2016 (online from late 2015), Routledge hardcover 2018; the 2017 date in the original lead is not used.

proposed_edges.relationship: In ‘A Long Atlantic in a Wider World’ (2004), Gabaccia urged greater engagement with literary and cultural scholarship in Atlantic history’s interdisciplinary dialogue, as William Boelhower explains in his 2016 assessment of Atlantic studies.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Boelhower’s substantive account and bibliography on the publisher’s page. The supporting phrase is his quotation from Gabaccia. Her original article remains unread after its publisher page returned 403; no individual scholar’s debt is inferred.
proposed_edges.map_label: An interdisciplinary agenda for Atlantic history
